planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Robin's plantain spreads gently by stolons and self-seeding to form a low, weed-suppressing patch along woodland edges and shaded lawns.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tolerates light foot traffic and mowing after bloom, making it a good native alternative to lawn in lightly shaded areas. Erigeron pulchellus (Robin's plantain) is a low, spreading native perennial of open woods, meadows, and woodland edges across eastern North America, forming rosettes of soft, hairy, spoon-shaped leaves that stay low and semi-evergreen through much of the year. In mid-spring, slender stems rise above the foliage carrying cheerful, daisy-like flowers with thin, numerous lavender-to-pink-tinged white rays around a bright yellow center — an important early nectar source for native bees and small butterflies, appearing alongside the earliest spring wildflowers. It spreads gently by both stolons and self-seeding into an attractive, low-maintenance patch without becoming aggressive, and it tolerates part shade as well as more open, sunny sites. A cheerful, easy native for the front of a woodland-edge border or naturalized meadow planting in zone 3–8.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, cold-moist stratifying for 30 days first, and transplant into average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after frost has passed; downy skullcap tolerates a wide range of light conditions from open woodland edge to full prairie sun.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; drought-tolerant once established and tends to flop in overly rich or shady sites, so lean soil and good light produce the sturdiest plants. Scutellaria incana is a tall native mint-family perennial of open woodlands, savannas, and prairie edges across the eastern and central United States, named for the fine, soft, gray-white down covering its stems and the undersides of its leaves. In mid-to-late summer, branching spikes crowded with small, hooded, blue-violet flowers rise well above the foliage, providing a long bloom period that is a magnet for bumblebees and other native pollinators. Its height and airy branching habit make it a good back-of-border native for a sunny to lightly shaded wildflower meadow or woodland-edge planting, where it combines well with other prairie and savanna natives. Zone 4–8.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or very early spring while dormant, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Double Bloodroot is sterile and spreads only slowly by rhizome, never by seed, so start with nursery-propagated divisions rather than expecting it to naturalize on its own.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; let the foliage die back naturally in early summer as the plant goes dormant, and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes. Sanguinaria canadensis 'Multiplex' is a showy double-flowered form of the native spring ephemeral bloodroot, bearing fully doubled, camellia-like white blooms with dozens of narrow petals in place of the single flower's simple eight to twelve petals. Because the flower is sterile and produces no seed, it never triggers the rapid petal drop that ends the single form's bloom within a day or two of opening — the double flowers instead persist attractively for one to two weeks, a significant advantage for garden display. Like the species, each striking, blue-green, deeply lobed leaf wraps protectively around its flower stem as it emerges in earliest spring; the cut rhizome exudes the characteristic red-orange sap that gives the plant its common name. A prized, long-lived heirloom woodland perennial for a shaded native garden, zone 3–8.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, cold-moist stratifying for 60 days first, or transplant divisions in spring or fall, into average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerant of dry shade once established, a valuable trait for planting beneath established trees. Cynoglossum virginianum (wild comfrey, or wild hound's tongue) is a native woodland perennial of the eastern United States, forming a basal rosette of large, coarse, hairy, tongue-shaped leaves — the source of its common name — from which a branching flower stalk rises in mid-spring, carrying loose clusters of small, pale blue to lavender, forget-me-not-like flowers. It is an unassuming but reliable early to mid-spring bloomer for the dry shade beneath hardwoods, a notoriously difficult site for many perennials, and its coarse foliage provides useful textural contrast to finer-leaved woodland companions like ferns and sedges. After flowering, the plant produces bur-like seed clusters that cling to fur and clothing for dispersal, in the manner typical of the borage family. A tough, easy native for a naturalistic dry shade garden, zone 4–8.

planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface in fall (seed needs light and a period of cool, moist conditions to germinate), into very well-drained, thin, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; widow's cross self-seeds readily once established and naturalizes best in a spot mimicking its native rock-outcrop habitat.

directions: Sow or set out in very well-drained, thin, lean, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant and intolerant of rich soil, competition, or standing moisture. Sedum pulchellum (widow's cross) is a diminutive native succulent of glades, granite and limestone rock outcrops, and thin prairie soils across the central and southeastern United States, forming low, spreading mats of narrow, cylindrical, bright green leaves that often blush red in dry, sunny conditions. In late spring to early summer, the plant sends up distinctive flower clusters arranged in a four-branched, cross-like pattern (the source of the common name), each branch lined with small, star-shaped, pink to rose-purple flowers that draw in small native bees and other pollinators. As a true annual or biennial, it completes its life cycle in a single season or two and relies on self-seeding to persist, readily colonizing bare rocky or gravelly ground where little else will grow. An excellent, easy, true-to-habitat choice for a rock garden, green roof, or gravel bed in zone 5–9.
